script.opening: “Hi doctor. I’ve had diarrhoea for nearly a week now since I went to Morocco, and there’s blood in it. The walk-in centre said it was a bug, but it’s not getting better and I need to be back at work Saturday.”

facts.text: “My cousin’s wedding in Marrakech. Four days of food — buffets, street stalls, everything.” Back three days. Started the day after the wedding.
“Six or seven times a day, watery, and the last two days there’s blood mixed in — sometimes streaks, once about a spoonful.” Some mucus. Cramps low down, mostly the left, eased after going.

“I get hot and sweaty at night. I haven’t got a thermometer.” If the doctor asks you to feel your forehead or look at you: you look tired but not grey. On video you can show the doctor your tongue — slightly dry.
“I’m drinking loads — water and the rehydration sachets my mum bought.” Passing urine normally, light yellow. No dizziness when standing. No vomiting.

facts.topic: Medicines (if asked what you have taken)
facts.text: “Paracetamol, and yesterday I got loperamide from the chemist to stop it — I took four.” Say this only if asked what you have taken or tried. No antibiotics recently, no hospital stays.
“My brother came too — he’s fine. I’m not sure about the other guests.” Lives with parents and younger sister; nobody else ill at home yet.
Never had anything like this before. No weight loss before the trip. No bruising, no reduced urine, no confusion.

facts.topic: Work (only if asked what you do)
facts.text: “I work in a café — I make the sandwiches and coffees.” If asked about pay: “Zero hours. If I don’t work, I don’t get paid. My manager says he’s short on Saturday and needs me.”

Be worried about the blood and about money. Mention the loperamide and the café only if asked. If told you cannot go to work, push back once: “I’ll just wear gloves.” Accept the advice if the doctor explains why and helps with the money problem (fit note, sick pay, Citizens Advice). Ask: “Can I go back to work on Saturday?”

ice.ideas: “Just a bad stomach bug from the food.”
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — He handles food on a zero-hours contract with no sick pay, his manager expects him on Saturday, and he took loperamide to “stop it” so he can work. Openly: the blood frightens him.
ice.expectations: Something to stop it quickly so he can go back to work at the weekend.

cues: “I need to be back at work Saturday.” — the occupational and money pressure.
“There’s blood in it.” — dysentery, not simple gastroenteritis.
“Something to stop it.” — he has already tried an antimotility drug.

checkpoints.text: Characterises the diarrhoea: duration, frequency, amount of blood and mucus, pain, fever, and travel and food history; checks contacts and recent antibiotics or hospital stays
Assesses severity and complications remotely: fluid intake, urine output, postural dizziness, vomiting; asks about reduced urine, bruising or pallor (haemolytic uraemic syndrome)
Asks what he has taken — finds the loperamide — and asks his occupation, finding he is a food handler

Arranges a stool sample (culture and ova, cysts and parasites, with travel history on the form) and bloods (FBC, U&E, CRP) within 24 hours; stops loperamide; no routine antibiotics while STEC is possible
Notifies suspected infectious bloody diarrhoea to the UKHSA health protection team and explains food-handler exclusion: 48 hours symptom-free, and possible clearance samples depending on the organism
Gives fluid and hygiene advice and specific safety-netting: increasing blood, severe pain, unable to keep fluids down, dizziness, passing little urine, confusion — same-day or 999
Recognises the money pressure and offers practical help (fit note, sick pay check, Citizens Advice) rather than simply forbidding work

worked.txt: “What have you taken so far — anything from the chemist to slow it down?”
“With blood and a temperature, slowing the gut down can keep the germ inside and make some infections more dangerous. Please stop the loperamide.”
“Most of these settle without antibiotics, and for one type of germ antibiotics can actually do harm. The stool test tells us which one it is — if you need treatment, I’ll ring you.”

“Because you make food for other people, the rule is no food handling until you’ve had 48 hours with no diarrhoea — and depending on the germ, the health protection team may want clear samples first. I know that hits your pay; let’s sort a fit note and look at what you’re entitled to.”

f.learning: Bloody diarrhoea with fever after travel is dysentery until proved otherwise, not “a bug”. Send stool for culture and ova, cysts and parasites with the travel history; check FBC, U&E and CRP when there is blood (dehydration, and STEC can cause haemolytic uraemic syndrome, usually 5–10 days after onset). Avoid antimotility drugs such as loperamide in bloody diarrhoea or high fever, and do not give antibiotics routinely — many cases are self-limiting and antibiotics may increase HUS risk with STEC; discuss with microbiology if he is systemically unwell or a result needs treatment. Infectious bloody diarrhoea is a notifiable condition: the GP notifies the health protection team on clinical suspicion, without waiting for the laboratory. Food handlers are excluded until 48 hours after symptoms stop, and some organisms (for example STEC, typhoid, some Shigella) need microbiological clearance as directed by the health protection team. Malaria and enteric fever must be considered in any febrile traveller returning from a risk area — here Morocco carries no malaria risk, but ask the itinerary.

knowledge.summary: Dysentery after travel: stool culture and OCP, bloods, stop loperamide, no routine antibiotics, notify, exclude from food handling and safety-net — while helping with the money pressure.

points.t: Blood or pus in the stool, recent travel abroad, systemic illness, immunocompromise, recent antibiotics or hospital admission (C. difficile), diarrhoea over 7 days, or a food handler or other high-risk occupation. Write the travel history on the form so the lab adds ova, cysts and parasites.

Campylobacter, Shigella, non-typhoidal Salmonella, STEC (E. coli O157 and others) and, less commonly, amoebic dysentery (Entamoeba histolytica). Enteric fever more often causes fever, headache and constipation than bloody diarrhoea.

Antimotility drugs (loperamide) with blood in the stool or high fever. NSAIDs while dehydrated. Empirical antibiotics while STEC is possible — seek microbiology advice if systemically unwell or immunocompromised.

Mostly after STEC: pallor, bruising or petechiae, reduced urine, drowsiness, typically 5–10 days after diarrhoea starts. FBC (anaemia, low platelets) and U&E (rising creatinine) are the screen; same-day hospital assessment if present.
Infectious bloody diarrhoea and food poisoning are notifiable on clinical suspicion. The registered medical practitioner notifies the local UKHSA health protection team; urgent cases by telephone.

Everyone: stay off work or school until 48 hours after the last episode. Food handlers and other risk groups: the health protection team may require negative samples for some organisms before return. Hygiene: hand-washing with soap and water (alcohol gel does not kill all organisms), no shared towels, clean toilet handles.
The Clear pass candidate asks what he has taken and what he does for work — and turns the exclusion advice into a plan he can actually afford to follow.

model.text: Hi Yusuf, it’s Dr Okafor. Can you see and hear me? I’ve read the walk-in centre letter. Tell me how things are now.
model.why: Uses the record and opens openly

model.text: Still going, six or seven times a day, and there’s blood now. I need to be back at work Saturday.
How much blood, and is there mucus? Any pain, and have you felt feverish?
Streaks, once a spoonful. Some slime. Cramps on the left. Hot and sweaty at night.
Are you keeping fluids down and passing urine normally? Any dizziness standing up, bruising, or feeling very drowsy?
Drinking loads, weeing fine, no dizziness, no bruises.
What have you taken for it so far? And what do you do for work?
Paracetamol, and four loperamide yesterday. I make sandwiches and coffee in a café.

With blood and a fever this is more than an ordinary tummy bug — it’s an infection of the bowel lining, probably picked up from food on the trip. I’d like a stool sample today and some blood tests tomorrow morning. Please stop the loperamide — slowing things down can make some of these infections worse.
Can’t I just have antibiotics to stop it?

Most settle without them, and for one type of germ antibiotics can do harm. Once the sample is back we’ll know — if you need treatment, I’ll call you. Keep up the sachets and fluids, paracetamol for the temperature, not ibuprofen.

About Saturday — because you handle food, the rule is no work until you’ve had 48 hours with no diarrhoea, and the health protection team, who I have to inform about bloody diarrhoea, may want clear samples first. I know that’s hard with zero hours. I’ll give you a fit note, and it’s worth checking with your employer or Citizens Advice about sick pay.
model.why: Exclusion, notification, and practical help with money

model.text: OK. I didn’t realise. I’ll tell my manager.

If the blood increases, the pain gets bad, you can’t keep fluids down, you feel faint, you’re passing much less urine, or you notice bruising — call 111 or go to A&E; 999 if you collapse. I’ll ring you with the results. Can you tell me the plan back?
Sample today, bloods tomorrow, stop the loperamide, no work till 48 hours clear, and A&E if it gets worse.

social.t: Zero-hours workers without sick pay are under pressure to return early — a real public health risk in food handling. Address income, not just infection control.
Lives with parents and a younger sister: hygiene advice protects them; anyone else who becomes ill should also be tested if they handle food or work with vulnerable people.

legal.t: Registered medical practitioners must notify suspected infectious bloody diarrhoea and food poisoning to the proper officer (UKHSA health protection team) without waiting for laboratory confirmation.

professional.t: The UTC impression was reasonable two days ago; new blood and persisting fever change the picture. Re-assess rather than inherit a label.

community.t: Citizens Advice (sick pay and benefits); NHS information on diarrhoea and vomiting; travel health advice before future trips (food and water hygiene).

redFlags: Signs of dehydration: dizziness, little urine, unable to keep fluids down
Immunocompromise; recent antibiotics or hospital stay
ice: Expectation: something to stop it so he can work

playbook.diagnosis: Acute infective bloody diarrhoea (dysentery) after travel to Morocco — probably bacterial (Campylobacter, Shigella, Salmonella or STEC); clinically stable; food handler.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “This is an infection of the lining of the bowel, probably from food on the trip. It usually settles, but the blood means we need to find out which germ it is.”

management.reflectIce: “You need to get back to work and you can’t afford time off. I want to help you do that safely — for you and for the people you make food for.”
management.psychosocial: Fit note; sick pay check; Citizens Advice; tell the manager the exclusion rule.
sharedPlan: Stool culture and OCP today (travel history on the form)
Stop loperamide; no antibiotics unless results or microbiology advice say so
Notify UKHSA health protection team; food-handler exclusion until 48 hours symptom-free and any clearance required
safetyNet: Increasing blood, severe pain, unable to keep fluids down, dizziness, little urine, bruising or drowsiness — 111 or A&E same day; 999 if collapse
Review if not settling within a week

pitfalls.intro: The UTC label of “gastroenteritis” invites a repeat of “fluids and wait”. The station is about the blood, the medicine he has taken, and the job he does.

items.fail: Never asks what he has taken or what he does for work.
items.why: Loperamide in dysentery can worsen outcomes, and a food handler with a notifiable infection is a public health risk.
items.fix: Ask “What have you tried?” and “What do you do for work?” in every diarrhoea history.

items.fail: Prescribes ciprofloxacin “to be safe” without a stool sample.
items.why: Antibiotics are not routinely needed, may raise HUS risk with STEC, and resistance is common.
items.fix: Stool sample first; seek microbiology advice if systemically unwell.

items.fail: Says “You can’t work, end of” and moves on.
items.why: Without help with income he is likely to go in anyway.
items.fix: Explain why, then help with the fit note and sick pay.

timeMap.d: Acknowledge the UTC letter; hear the work deadline.
Blood, fever, pain; hydration and HUS screen; what he has taken; occupation; contacts.
Dysentery; stool sample and bloods; stop loperamide; no routine antibiotics.
Notification, 48-hour exclusion and clearance, fit note and sick pay, red flags, teach-back.

wordPics.clearFail: Accepts “gastroenteritis”, advises fluids only, misses the loperamide and occupation, or prescribes antibiotics and lets him return Saturday.
wordPics.fail: Requests a stool sample but does not stop the loperamide, does not notify, or gives generic return-to-work advice without the food-handler rule.
wordPics.pass: Takes a focused history, arranges stool and bloods, stops loperamide, avoids routine antibiotics, notifies, explains food-handler exclusion and safety-nets clearly.
wordPics.clearPass: All of the Pass, plus: screens for HUS in plain words, explains each decision so he agrees with it, handles the money pressure practically, and confirms the plan by teach-back.

avoid.dont: “Keep taking the loperamide if it helps you get through work.”
avoid.instead: “Please stop the loperamide — with blood and fever it can make things worse.”
avoid.why: Antimotility agents are avoided in dysentery.

avoid.dont: “Just wear gloves and you’ll be fine.”
avoid.instead: “Food handlers need 48 hours clear — and sometimes clear samples — before going back.”
avoid.why: Gloves do not prevent transmission of these organisms.

avoid.instead: “It’s an infection of the bowel lining — we need to find out which germ.”
avoid.why: Blood and fever change the management.

Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.

Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.
